headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers - one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper - and does not describe either condition in general.

Both papers show that more severe or more persistent illness costs substantially more than milder illness, but they measure cost in different ways (direct medical/non-medical cost in euros for Lyme disease versus lost labor income in dollars for Long COVID), so the two cannot be converted into one number.

Both papers flag that their national totals are built from pooled averages with no breakdown by age, sex, race, or disability, and both explicitly warn that real-world burden is likely higher than what they capture.

comparison_rows.dimension: What type of economic burden is measured

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper models direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), and productivity loss together, estimating a total annual national cost of EUR 5,592,056 (2019 price year).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper measures only lost labor cost from missed workdays among full-time workers, estimating a projected national lost labor cost of USD 12,784,168,675.20 (2022 price year); it does not measure direct medical costs at all.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Readers should not combine or compare these totals directly, since they cover different cost categories, different currencies, and different price years.

comparison_rows.dimension: Cost gradient tied to severity or persistence

lyme.finding: Disseminated/late-stage Lyme disease costs 26.67 times as much per patient as early-stage disease (ratio, 2019 price year), and disseminated/late-stage cases drive 62% of the total national cost despite being less common.

long_covid.finding: People with Long COVID had USD 1,242.04 (2022) higher mean lost labor cost per individual than people who never had COVID-19, and USD 478.91 (2022) higher than people who had COVID-19 without Long COVID.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers independently show that the more severe or longer-lasting form of each condition carries a disproportionately larger cost burden, even though the dollar/euro figures themselves are not comparable.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports patient out-of-pocket cost as a share of total per-patient cost: 22.75% for early-stage patients versus 5.56% for disseminated/late-stage patients (2019 price year), and states overall 75.5% of direct medical costs were reimbursed by insurance.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report any patient out-of-pocket cost figures.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper lets a reader see how much of the financial burden falls on patients themselves versus insurers.

lyme.finding: In the Lyme disease paper, productivity loss (indirect non-medical cost) makes up 46.4% of the total national cost (2019 price year), with disseminated/late-stage ambulatory patients losing on average EUR 2,432-3,341 per patient depending on PTLDS status.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's entire estimate is built on work and income loss: mean lost labor cost was USD 1,944.46 per individual with Long COVID versus USD 702.42 for those who never had COVID-19 (2022 price year), but it captures only missed workdays (absenteeism), not reduced productivity while working or people who left the workforce.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers treat work loss as an important burden component, but Lyme disease treats it as one slice of a broader cost total while the Long COVID paper treats it as the whole analysis, so the scope of what counts as 'burden' differs substantially.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports only pooled national and group-level averages, with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper likewise reports only pooled national/group-level totals and means, with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or veteran status.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper can tell a reader whether the economic burden falls more heavily on particular demographic groups within each condition.

comparison_rows.dimension: How official/administrative data may undercount the condition

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states there is no specific ICD-10-CM code for erythema migrans or post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, so hospital costs for those presentations were folded into the broader disseminated/late-stage category, and coding quality could not be verified.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper relies on self-reported COVID-19/Long COVID history and self-reported missed workdays, which the study's own authors note may lead to under- or overestimation, and there is no direct measure isolating sick days specifically caused by Long COVID.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers rely on data sources (administrative coding or self-report) that their own authors flag as an imperfect match to true clinical reality, meaning both estimates carry real but differently-sourced uncertainty.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper explicitly excludes costs occurring beyond 6-12 months post-diagnosis, prophylactic treatment costs, and most non-reimbursed hospital supplement costs, warning that true burden is likely higher than reported.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper excludes people who left the workforce entirely or dropped below full-time hours because of Long COVID, as well as direct medical costs, caregiving costs, and presenteeism, meaning its labor-cost estimate likely understates total burden.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers' authors acknowledge real gaps that likely push the true economic burden of each condition above the published figures.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 75.5% of direct medical costs were reimbursed by health insurance overall, with non-reimbursed costs making up 24.5 percentage points of direct medical costs (2019 price year).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that 79.6% of people with Long COVID had paid sick leave, and found no statistically significant association between having paid sick leave and having Long COVID (odds ratio 0.90, p=.51).

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers measure different kinds of coverage (health insurance reimbursement versus paid sick leave), so a reader cannot conclude which condition's patients are better protected financially from this evidence alone.

shared_themes.theme: In both papers, the more severe or longer-persisting form of the condition carries a disproportionately larger per-person economic cost than the milder or shorter form.

evidence.note: Disseminated/late-stage Lyme disease costs 26.67 times as much per patient as early-stage (erythema migrans) disease, 2019 price year.
Mean lost labor cost was USD 1,242.04 higher for people with Long COVID than for those who never had COVID-19, 2022 price year.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers present only pooled national or group-level cost figures without any demographic subgroup breakdown, so neither can show whether burden differs by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability.

evidence.note: National and per-patient cost figures are reported with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status.
National and per-individual lost labor cost figures are reported with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability, or veteran status.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers openly acknowledge that their published cost estimates leave out real burdens, meaning the true economic impact of each condition is likely understated.

evidence.note: Costs beyond 6-12 months post-diagnosis and most non-reimbursed hospital supplement costs are excluded from the EUR 5.59 million national total.
People who left the workforce or dropped below full-time hours because of Long COVID are excluded from the lost labor cost estimate.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper shows that even though a large majority of direct medical costs are reimbursed by insurance, early-stage patients bear a much larger out-of-pocket share of their (much smaller) total cost than late-stage patients do.

evidence.note: Early-stage (erythema migrans) patients' out-of-pocket share of total per-patient cost was 22.75% versus 5.56% for disseminated/late-stage patients, 2019 price year.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper identifies a specific administrative data gap: no distinct billing code exists for erythema migrans or post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, so hospital costs for these presentations cannot be separated from the broader disseminated/late-stage category.

evidence.note: No specific ICD-10-CM code exists for erythema migrans or PTLDS, so related hospital costs were folded into the disseminated/late-stage group.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper captures only missed workdays (absenteeism) and explicitly does not measure reduced productivity while still working (presenteeism) or workers who left the labor force entirely.

evidence.note: The paper states presenteeism is not measured and the study population is restricted to full-time workers (35-100 hrs/week), excluding those who reduced hours or left work.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper finds no statistically significant relationship between having paid sick leave and having Long COVID, suggesting paid leave access does not clearly explain differences in lost labor cost.

evidence.note: Unadjusted odds ratio for paid sick leave and Long COVID status was 0.90 (95% CI 0.66-1.23, p=.51), not statistically significant.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither the Lyme disease paper nor the Long COVID paper breaks down its cost estimates by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status, so neither can show whether burden differs across these groups.
Neither paper measures caregiving time or caregiver financial burden as part of its cost estimate.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers - one on Lyme disease in Belgium and one on Long COVID in US full-time workers - and does not describe either condition in general, since each conclusion rests on a single uploaded document. Both papers independently find that the more severe or more persistent form of the condition costs noticeably more per person, and both explicitly warn that their published totals likely undercount the true economic burden because of excluded time periods, excluded populations, or imperfect underlying data. However, the two papers measure fundamentally different things (Lyme disease: direct medical, non-medical, and productivity costs in 2019 euros; Long COVID: lost labor income only, in 2022 dollars), so their dollar/euro figures cannot be added, divided, or treated as equivalent. Neither paper provides any breakdown by demographic subgroup, leaving an open question in both cases about whether burden is distributed evenly across the population.
cross_analysis.limitations: This comparison rests on a small, non-random sample: exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, each built from a single uploaded source document, with no papers available that cover both conditions together. This is not a controlled study, and the findings should not be generalized beyond what each individual paper's own data and stated scope support.

learning_cards.headline: Late-stage Lyme costs 26.67 times more per patient than early care
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper reports that disseminated/late-stage disease costs 26.67 times as much per patient as early-stage (EM) disease, in 2019 euros.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not measure direct medical costs at all, only lost labor income, so it cannot say how much a more severe or prolonged presentation adds to care costs.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers estimate whether patients with longer-lasting symptoms incur disproportionately higher direct medical costs, similar to the late-stage multiple seen in the Lyme disease paper?

learning_cards.headline: Patients cover more of their own costs early, not late
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper finds patient out-of-pocket share is 22.75% of total per-patient cost for early-stage disease but only 5.56% for disseminated/late-stage disease.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not track out-of-pocket spending at any stage, so it cannot compare how much of the financial burden falls on the patient versus the system.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Should Long COVID cost studies add an out-of-pocket spending measure to see whether early or persistent cases shift more of the financial burden onto patients themselves?

learning_cards.headline: Lost income is largest compared with never having had the illness
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper reports a mean lost labor cost gap of 1242.04 USD versus people who never had COVID-19, compared with a smaller gap of 478.91 USD versus people who had COVID-19 without Long COVID.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not measure lost labor income at any stage, so it cannot say how much disseminated or early-stage Lyme disease affects a person's earnings.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers estimate whether disseminated/late-stage patients lose more labor income than early-stage patients or than people who were never diagnosed?

learning_cards.headline: A national lost-income total exists for Long COVID, not for Lyme
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper projects a national lost labor cost of 12784168675.2 USD attributable to Long COVID in 2022.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper reports a national cost figure only for disseminated/late-stage disease (3467074.72 EUR/year) and this covers direct and related costs, not lost labor income specifically.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Belgian Lyme disease researchers produce a national lost labor cost estimate comparable in scope to the Long COVID paper's 12784168675.2 USD figure?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper could prompt Long COVID researchers to examine direct medical costs and who pays out-of-pocket at different stages, while the Long COVID paper could prompt Lyme disease researchers to examine lost labor income as its own measured burden.
